headline: Texas used $1 car insurance fee to fund 3,200+ Flock surveillance cameras statewide
summary: A state agency used $30M from a $1 annual auto insurance fee, originally for catalytic converter theft, to install over 3,200 Flock cameras across Texas. Governor Abbott has now paused state funding for these grants.
details: In 2023, the Texas Legislature passed a law adding $1 to auto insurance policies to combat catalytic converter theft. However, a state agency has since devoted at least $30 million of this fee to expand the state's Flock surveillance network, installing over 3,200 cameras.

The Motor Vehicle Crime Prevention Authority, with a board largely appointed by Governor Greg Abbott, oversaw the distribution of these funds. The agency aimed to use the fee increase to 'cover the entire state' with cameras.

The authority awarded over 95 grants to law enforcement agencies, facilitating the purchase and maintenance of approximately 2,000 Flock cameras. An additional $15.9 million supported the Texas Department of Public Safety in adding nearly 1,200 more cameras.

Further expansion was planned, with another $3 million approved for DPS to install 583 more cameras along Texas tollways. Laredo Police Chief Miguel Rodriguez, chair of the authority, views these cameras as a powerful tool against criminal organizations.

Following inquiries from The Texas Tribune, Governor Abbott's office announced a pause on all state funding for local grants used for Flock cameras. His spokesperson clarified that state agencies are ensuring funds cannot be used for these devices.

The $1 annual fee has generated an estimated $81 million, with $50.8 million allocated to 234 grants. These grants also reimbursed police departments for officers, crime analysts, attorneys, drones, and other surveillance equipment.

The widespread deployment of Flock cameras has sparked backlash and privacy concerns, even among some legislators who initially approved the $1 fee. Lawmakers like Rep. Mitch Little question the Fourth Amendment implications of the captured data volume.

State Senator Carol Alvarado and Rep. Jeff Leach, who sponsored the original bill, expressed surprise upon learning the insurance fee was funding AI-supported license plate readers. They stated surveillance cameras were not discussed during the bill's consideration.

headline_marked: [[Build an AI-Powered Sleep Apnea Monitor]] with Whisper-v3 & Librosa
headline: Build an AI-Powered Sleep Apnea Monitor with Whisper-v3 & Librosa
summary: Learn to build a high-fidelity sleep apnea and snore monitoring system using Whisper-v3, Librosa, and PyAudio, enabling real-time detection and noise filtering.
details: Unlock the secrets of your sleep by building a high-fidelity Sleep Apnea and Snore Monitoring system. This DIY project leverages Whisper-v3, Librosa, and PyAudio to provide insights into your nightly rest without expensive clinic visits.

The system tackles complex audio processing, real-time sleep apnea detection, and advanced audio fingerprinting. It can distinguish between ambient noise, rhythmic snoring, and critical respiratory pauses, which standard noise-canceling often misses.

Audio is captured in chunks, with Librosa used to calculate Root Mean Square (RMS) energy to avoid processing hours of silence. This efficient approach ensures only relevant sound blocks are analyzed.

To manage Whisper-v3's computational demands, a lightweight Audio Fingerprint (MFCCs) 'wakes up' the AI only when specific breathing patterns are detected. This optimizes performance for continuous monitoring.

Sleep apnea is identified by tracking pauses in breathing using a rolling window. If MFCC energy drops below a threshold for over 10 seconds, followed by a high-frequency spike (a gasp), an apnea event is flagged.
The entire system is designed to run on compact devices like a Raspberry Pi or home server. Docker is utilized to simplify deployment and manage dependencies, ensuring portability and ease of setup.

While this DIY monitor offers an incredible learning experience, deploying health-tech requires rigorous validation. For production-grade, HIPAA-compliant architectures, resources like WellAlly Blog offer advanced insights into AI reliability and edge computing.
